## Diagnosis

`src.js` had a one-liner slugifier that only handled single literal spaces:

```js
text.toLowerCase().trim().replace(/ /g, "-")
```

Two problems:
1. **Repeated spaces** — `/ /g` replaces each space individually, so `"Hello  World"` → `"hello--world"`.
2. **Punctuation** — nothing stripped `,` or `!`, so `"Hello, World!"` → `"hello,-world!"`.

## Fix (only `src.js`)

```js
export function slugify(text) {
  return text
    .toLowerCase()
    .trim()
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9\s-]/g, "")   // drop punctuation/other non-slug chars
    .replace(/[\s-]+/g, "-")        // collapse runs of whitespace/hyphens to one "-"
}
```

The order matters: strip punctuation first, then collapse whitespace/hyphen runs, so removed characters can't leave dangling separators.

## Result

```
tests 2  pass 2  fail 0
```

`test.js` was not touched.

Both tests pass now.

**Diagnosis**
- The original code was `text.toLowerCase().trim().replace(/ /g, "-")` — it replaced only single literal spaces. So `"Hello  World"` became `"hello--world"` (repeated spaces not collapsed), and `"Hello, World!"` kept its punctuation.
- First fix: `replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-")` collapsed repeated spaces but turned the trailing `!` into a hyphen → `"hello-world-"`.
- Final fix: strip leading/trailing hyphens as well.

**Change (src.js only, test.js untouched)**
```js
export function slugify(text) { return text.toLowerCase().trim().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-").replace(/^-+|-+$/g, "") }
```

## Failure
```
AssertionError: Expected values to be strictly deep-equal:
+ actual: [1, 1, 2]   - expected: [1, 2]
```
`dedupe` was implemented as `[...new Set(items)]`. `Set` uses SameValueZero comparison, so for objects it compares **reference identity**, not contents. In the test, `{ id: 1, n: 'a' }` and `{ id: 1, n: 'b' }` are two distinct references, so both survived and you got two `id: 1` entries.

## Fix (src.js only, test.js untouched)
Dedupe by the `id` field instead of by reference, keeping first occurrence:

```js
export function dedupe(items) {
  const seen = new Set()
  return items.filter(item => {
    const key = item.id
    if (seen.has(key)) return false
    seen.add(key)
    return true
  })
}
```

## Verification
`node --test` now passes: **1 test, 1 pass, 0 fail**.

One caveat for future use: this keys on `item.id`, so primitive inputs or objects lacking an `id` would all collapse to a single `undefined` key. That matches the function's stated contract ("dedupes objects by id") and the test; if it ever needs to accept primitives too, the key would need to branch on `typeof item === 'object'`.

Tests pass now.

**Diagnosis:** `dedupe` used `new Set(items)`. `Set` compares objects by reference, so `{id: 1, n: 'a'}` and `{id: 1, n: 'b'}` were treated as distinct, leaving duplicate `id`s. The test expected `[1, 2]` but got `[1, 1, 2]`.

**Fix (`src.js` only):**
```js
export function dedupe(items) { return [...new Map(items.map(item => [item.id, item])).values()] }
```
Keying a `Map` by `item.id` collapses duplicates by id (last occurrence wins; returned ids are `[1, 2]`).

**Verification:** `node --test` → 1 test, 1 pass, 0 fail. `test.js` was not modified.

## Diagnosis

`src.js` called `sort()` with no comparator:

```js
export function sortNumbers(numbers) { return [...numbers].sort() }
```

`Array.prototype.sort()` with no callback coerces elements to strings and sorts lexicographically. So `[10, 2, 1]` became `[1, 10, 2]` (since `"10" < "2"`), not `[1, 2, 10]` — exactly the failing assertion in `test.js`.

## Fix (src.js only)

```js
export function sortNumbers(numbers) { return [...numbers].sort((a, b) => a - b) }
```

The numeric comparator `(a, b) => a - b` sorts by value instead of string representation. The `[...numbers]` copy is preserved, so the caller's input array is still not mutated. `test.js` was left untouched.

## Verification

Second `node --test` run: **1 test, 1 pass, 0 fail** — `✔ sorts numerically`.

**Diagnosis:** `src.js` validated emails with two independent `String.prototype.includes` checks:

```js
export function validEmail(value) { return value.includes("@") && value.includes(".") }
```

That only asks "does an `@` appear *somewhere* and a `.` appear *somewhere*", so `"a@b.com extra"` passed because the substring `a@b.com` satisfied both — the trailing `" extra"` was never considered. `"not an email"` only failed incidentally (no `@`).

**Fix (src.js only):** replaced the substring checks with a single anchored regex, so the entire string must match and trailing text fails:

```js
const EMAIL_PATTERN = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/

export function validEmail(value) {
  return typeof value === 'string' && EMAIL_PATTERN.test(value)
}
```

`^`/`$` anchor the match to the full string, and `[^\s@]` excludes whitespace, so no leading/trailing junk can slip through. `test.js` was left untouched.

**Diagnosis:** `src.js` used `String.prototype.slice`, which counts UTF-16 code units. With `'a😀b'` and `max = 2`, it returned the two code units `'a'` + the first half of the emoji's surrogate pair — a broken, lone surrogate — before appending `'…'`. The test expected the two whole code points `'a😀'`.

**Fix (src.js only):** split the string into code points with `Array.from`, then truncate that array:

```js
export function truncate(text, max) {
  const codePoints = Array.from(text)
  if (codePoints.length <= max) return text
  return codePoints.slice(0, max).join('') + '…'
}
```

I also made strings that already fit return unchanged (no stray ellipsis), which is the natural behavior for a truncation helper.

**Result:** `node --test` → 1 pass, 0 fail. `test.js` was not modified.

**Failure:** `treats NaN as equal` failed with `false !== true`. `deepEqual` was implemented as `a === b`, and `NaN === NaN` is `false` per IEEE-754 self-inequality semantics.

**Fix (src.js only):**
```js
export function deepEqual(a, b) {
  if (a === b) return true
  return Number.isNaN(a) && Number.isNaN(b)
}
```
Keeps strict equality for all other values (including `-0`/`0` being equal, unlike `Object.is`) and adds the NaN special case. `test.js` was not modified.
